On three established benchmarks (BIRD, Spider, Mini-Dev) spanning over 3,000 evaluation instances, three SQL dialects (SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL), and six model configurations, Post-SQLFix resolves 77.8% of the execution errors that EF leaves unrepaired, while requiring less than half as many repair iterations and 30% fewer tokens. Crucially, accepted transitions under the monitor introduce no statically detectable structural regressions in our evaluation, translating checked repair fidelity into absolute accuracy improvements of up to +11.6 percentage points.

arxiv:2611.00163.title: Claude for Excel is Transformative for Basic Spreadsheet Modeling and Analysis
arxiv:2611.00163.abstract: We used the Claude Excel plug-in to build and analyze spreadsheet models for five semi structured problem statements (including a test-piece teaching case with data in multiple exhibits) and evaluated performance on modeling (what is to be coded), spreadsheet engineering (quality of coding), analysis (algorithms applied to the spreadsheet), and insight generation. Claude's ability to create a high-quality spreadsheet model from a semi structured problem statement is astoundingly excellent. Given very simple prompts, Claude generates extensive, accurate sensitivity and scenario analyses and reasonable plain English insights. Claude is Solver-aware and builds optimization models without specific prompting. Analyst productivity gains will likely be high. Business school quant courses will have to change. The way we develop human expertise will have to change.
arxiv:2611.00163.journal_ref: Proceedings of the EuSpRIG 2026 conference 'Spreadsheets, AI Agents, Trust, and Governance' ISBN 9781-905404-61-2 Copyright 2026, European Spreadsheet Risks Interest Group and Authors

arxiv:2610.41562.title: SCRBench: Beyond Equivalence Checking for Semantic Change Reasoning in Code
arxiv:2610.41562.abstract: Understanding how code changes affect program semantics is a core aspect of code reasoning in language models. It is commonly evaluated by asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, but a yes/no answer does not reveal whether a model knows which code change caused a semantic difference, or which sequence of code changes produced the modified program. We study two tasks that ask these questions directly, diagnosing semantic change and reconstructing sequences of code changes, alongside detecting semantic equivalence. We build SCRBench, 67,658 Python program pairs generated by applying sequences of code changes that preserve or alter program semantics, and evaluate five language models on a stratified subset of 4,500 pairs. Detecting semantic equivalence exposes weaker models, whose accuracy declines as changes accumulate, but the strongest models remain near the ceiling. Diagnosing semantic change reveals weaknesses that equivalence accuracy hides: a model with 94.71% equivalence accuracy diagnoses only 54.44% of semantic changes. Reconstructing sequences of code changes is much harder: the best model reconstructs the exact sequence for only 39.27% of pairs, and no model exceeds 1.11% when five changes are applied. High equivalence accuracy therefore overestimates how well models reason about the semantic effects of code changes.

arxiv:2610.41617.title: Prompt Less, Infer More: Static Analysis-Guided LLM Type Annotation for Python
arxiv:2610.41617.abstract: Type annotations improve the maintainability and reliability of Python programs, but many real-world projects remain under-annotated because manual annotation is time-consuming and error-prone. Recent neural and LLM-based type inference systems can recover missing annotations, yet they often trade accuracy for efficiency. Existing approaches often fail to exploit project-wide type evidence, or do so inefficiently through unnecessary model calls and noisy prompts. We present SALT, an LLM-based type inference system guided by static analysis. SALT integrates static analysis with LLM inference to resolve types statically, prioritize LLM queries, and construct concise type-aware context. To demonstrate the effectiveness of SALT, we evaluated it on 12 real-world Python projects. SALT achieves the best accuracy among the evaluated systems and reduces estimated LLM cost by up to 78.5% compared with a strong coding-assistant baseline. It also shows similar cost savings with the frontier model GPT-5.5, demonstrating that SALT remains effective with strong LLMs.

arxiv:2610.41628.title: What Carries Architectural Signal? A Code-to-Architecture Mapping Study
arxiv:2610.41628.abstract: Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture. Representations of implementation artifacts can capture code text, dependencies, and directory organization, but predictive gains alone do not establish the contribution of additional graph processing. Dependencies may already be encoded in these representations, while directories may closely match the reference decomposition. We investigate how artifact representations and graph context affect mapping on ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget. We compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations and assess each predictor with and without dependency neighbors. Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), we compare file-level graphs extended with member nodes summarizing each file's program elements, folder nodes, or both, alongside a variant encoding folder paths directly in file representations. We compare folder-aware predictions with a directory rule using the same labeled files. Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical representations on most systems. Additional neighbor aggregation can improve mapping, depending on the predictor and aggregation direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains across the evaluated HGT configurations. However, the directory rule achieves per-system median accuracy of 89-100%, and adding folder information does not consistently improve predictions for files the rule misclassifies. Member nodes provide no consistent improvement over file-level graphs. These findings support assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide before attributing improvements to graph neural networks.

arxiv:2610.41685.title: A Failure Mode Taxonomy and Severity Model for Ethereum Smart Contracts
arxiv:2610.41685.abstract: Smart contracts are a core component of blockchain systems, but their immutability makes failures in deployed code catastrophic and irreversible. Existing work classifies vulnerabilities, defects, and attacks, yet the observable failures of smart contracts, the deviations from intended behavior or the expected ledger state seen once a contract is deployed, have been largely disregarded. In this paper, we design and validate a failure mode taxonomy for Ethereum smart contracts, together with a severity model that ranks failures by their observable impact. Using a literature review as input, we follow the taxonomy development method of Nickerson et al. to derive the failure modes and their dimensions, and we subject the resulting taxonomy to a saturation exercise over a systematic literature review, the OpenSCV vulnerability catalog, and smart contract incidents reported after the search cutoff. Each failure mode is characterized along five dimensions, namely root cause, violated security property, impact (recorded as primary, secondary, and other), affected component, and nature, and is given a standardized name targeting the observable malfunction rather than the underlying vulnerability. From the taxonomy, we derive CIPER, a five-level severity model that groups failure modes by their observable impact. The saturation exercise produced no new failure modes or dimensions. The taxonomy offers a shared vocabulary for describing what smart contracts do wrong when they fail, and CIPER links that vocabulary to the severity of each observable outcome.

arxiv:2610.41800.title: Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies
arxiv:2610.41800.abstract: Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair, and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair. Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs $0.55-$1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists.

arxiv:2610.41863.title: Stuck on Red? Understanding GitHub Actions Failing Streaks
arxiv:2610.41863.abstract: GitHub Actions is the de facto CI/CD service for GitHub repositories. Its workflows should not fail when they are not expected to, nor keep on failing too long. We empirically study failing streaks, i.e., uninterrupted series of failing runs of a workflow, in 30.9M+ runs of 154K+ workflows of 43K+ GitHub repositories over 238 days. We study how failing streaks begin and end, and what happens during them, based on the trigger and the commit of each run. We also classify all workflows by their purposes, such as building, testing or deploying, and we inspect the logs of a small sample of failing streaks. Failing runs mostly come in streaks: three quarters of them follow another failing run, and half of the workflows with at least three runs have at least one failing streak. Workflows serving multiple purposes have failing streaks more often, even at the same size. Most failing streaks end within hours, but the one in five that last more than a day account for the lion's share of the time that workflows spend failing. A third of the failing streaks start, and two in five end, without any change to the repository. In a sample of 100 failing streaks, those that end this way most often fail because of network issues or an external service. These findings suggest that maintainers should not assume that a failure comes from the last commit. GitHub and tool builders could flag failures that occur without any change to the repository, and alert the active maintainers when a workflow stays failing for more than a day.

arxiv:2610.41878.title: No More Import Errors: Constrained Decoding for Guaranteed Valid Imports in LLM-Generated Tests
arxiv:2610.41878.abstract: One of the most common failure reasons of LLM-based test generation pipelines is import errors. Grammar constrained decoding can modify the probabilities of the LLM's final layer during token generation to guarantee valid imports. However, we find that it can lead to degenerate solutions, i.e., repetitive valid imports (import streaks) that exhaust the token budget before a test is generated. We propose Constrained Beam Decoding with Lookup (CBDL), a novel method that guarantees import validity while addressing import streaks by avoiding premature commitment to tokens that lead to repetitive imports. Because it operates at the decoding stage, CBDL can be integrated into existing LLM-based test generation pipelines. We implement CBDL for Python and Java and evaluate it on two test generation tasks, showing that generated tests have 100% valid imports, outperforming both static (RAG and LIBRO) and dynamic (Agentic Repair) import-validity approaches that leave 45%, 10%, and 43% of import errors unresolved. CBDL converts on average 14% of initial import errors into functionally correct tests, increasing overall test correctness by 1-4 percentage points over unconstrained generation. Even when import validity does not directly lead to a correct test, it allows agentic repair pipelines to allocate the repair budget to remaining errors, increasing correct tests by 2-7 percentage points for Python and 1-6 for Java. Finally, we show that a hybrid pipeline, where a small local model equipped with CBDL generates imports while the frontier GPT-5.2 model generates the test body, outperforms generating both with GPT-5.2 alone by 1-3 percentage points. Overall, CBDL removes a major bottleneck in LLM-based test generation: by guaranteeing import validity with a small overhead (16-21 seconds per test), it improves test correctness and enables cost-effective hybrid generation.

arxiv:2610.42144.title: Dittany: Contribution-Guided Repair Framework for MAS Applications
arxiv:2610.42144.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent system (MAS) applications can produce useful intermediate results while leaving task requirements unsatisfied. Repairing such executions requires identifying the work still needed and the completed results that can support it. We present \tool, a contribution-guided runtime repair framework for MAS applications. \tool derives expected contributions and acceptance conditions from task requirements and method specifications, and connects their dependencies in a contribution graph. Runtime checks locate unmet conditions and establish which results remain usable. These results guide action-level correction when available inputs suffice, or graph-level recovery when prerequisites or unfinished work need revision. Both repair scopes retain validated contributions and check repaired outputs before subsequent work uses them. We evaluate \tool on 30 applications across six MAS frameworks and 9,000 tasks. It detects runtime failures with 88.28\% precision and 79.18\% recall, and achieves 84.76\% task accuracy, improving over Native execution by 26.74 percentage points and the strongest of four recovery baselines by 21.28 points. Estimated deployment token consumption is 17.92\% above Native, but 24.19\% below Reflexion and 13.05\% below Iterative Rollback. Ablation results show that combining the two repair scopes achieves higher accuracy and lower token consumption than graph-level repair alone.

arxiv:2611.00287.title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
arxiv:2611.00287.abstract: Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols. To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.

arxiv:2611.00294.title: Software Change Request in AI-Orchestrated Software Evolution: Literature Review and Research Agenda
arxiv:2611.00294.abstract: In the emerging paradigm of holistic AI-orchestrated software maintenance and evolution, large-scale app stores continuously generate exponentially vast Software Change Requests (SCRs) streams through user feedbacks. These streams enable intelligent software evolution. Automating SCR extraction and classification is crucial with rapid growth of Mobile Apps (MA). However, significant challenges exist such as scare large-scale datasets, inconsistent classification schemes, limited data sharing and insufficient research. This study presents a first and thorough systematic survey of SCR identification from MA Reviews (MAR). In particular, we investigated how Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) enhanced identification and classification of SCR. This study has found pertinent datasets varying sizes from 5,000 to more than 18 million reviews. The key findings highlight the dominant use of Random Forest and Support Vector Machines, limited adoption of deep learning techniques, inconsistent F1-score results ranging from 0.08 to 1 and partial automation in existing SCR tools such as SURF and ChangeAdvisor. Finally, we have performed a synthesis of the studies to presents a comparative taxonomy of SCR methodologies, identify research gaps and annotation frameworks. We contend that classification schemes, shared datasets and annotation frameworks are essential for advancing SCRs and thereby improving the maintenance of mobile applications.

arxiv:2611.00296.title: Hardware-Aware Conditional Code in Android Apps
arxiv:2611.00296.abstract: Android OS runs on a highly diverse set of devices, spanning entry-level phones and flagships with substantially different hardware characteristics, including memory capacity, processors, displays, cameras, and sensors. Through APIs, apps can query device information at runtime, such as memory, hardware features, and manufacturer, among other device properties, allowing developers to execute different code paths on different devices. Existing studies cover only specific compatibility bugs or brand-specific behavior; however, the broader use of hardware information in app logic has not been comprehensively explored. We address this question with a large-scale empirical study of hardware-related if statements in Android apps. We statically analyze 50,000 apps to identify the if statements whose conditions depend on the values of hardware-related APIs, and extract their conditions together with the code of their branches. Our results show that 95% of successfully analyzed apps contain at least one such statement, with an average of 74 per app, which suggests that hardware-related logic is widespread. We then apply an LLM-assisted open-coding process to the extracted code to build a structured taxonomy of the purposes behind hardware-related conditional code. The resulting characterization shows that developers use hardware information for feature availability checks, UI adaptation, emulator detection, device tiering, and resource management, among others.

arxiv:2611.00340.title: Autoformalization for Ambiguous Inputs: Precision, Coverage, and Cost across SQL and Logical Forms
arxiv:2611.00340.abstract: Agentic systems translate natural-language requests into executable artifacts while managing ambiguity and inference cost. We evaluate seven autoformalization workflows on SQL and first-order logic benchmarks for ambiguous inputs. Across five SQL workflows, the raw model leads with F1 of 53.35% on AMBROSIA and 60.85% on AmbiQT. On AmP, DRIFT gains 15.98 F1 points over the raw model at 2.03 times its token cost, whereas LoC uses 18.65 times the raw model's tokens with lower F1. Within AutoCedar, structured interpretation lowers F1 by 6.44-6.95 points and raises AMBROSIA token use 2.2-fold. Paired reviewer comparisons show modest Kimi K3 gains of 1.93 points on AMBROSIA and 2.04 on AmbiQT. Clear-ambiguous AMBROSIA analysis shows greater relative stability for AutoCedar, with a smaller F1 drop than the raw model (11.46 vs. 16.68 points), alongside lower aggregate F1 (50.16% vs. 53.35%). Autoformalization alone does not guarantee robustness to ambiguity: the tested additions offer no uniformly effective remedy, making accuracy, ambiguity handling, and inference cost joint design requirements.

arxiv:2611.00384.title: Agent Stack for ML Training Lifecycle: Generation, Validation, and Optimization
arxiv:2611.00384.abstract: Production model development requires repeated architecture design, platform integration, debugging, training, and evaluation. We present an agent stack deployed at LinkedIn with two independently usable agent loops: AutoTorch for model generation and migration, and AutoResearch for model optimization. AutoTorch generates PyTorch models and training pipelines for TensorFlow migration, XGBoost replacement, and new-model development. Executable validation hooks check platform API compliance, trainability, and conversion fidelity on sampled data, guiding iterative repair before engineer review and full-scale distributed training. AutoResearch explores architecture and training-configuration changes through expert-steered or autonomous experimentation. An external orchestrator manages parallel trials, experiment history, candidate selection, and wall-clock budgets across agent sessions. A shared runtime preserves execution state independently of agent reasoning and allocates GPUs separately from agent execution. Across ranking, content understanding, and recommendation workloads, AutoTorch completed generation and full-scale training in 92 of 115 workflow runs (80%). Of these, 77 (83.7%) produced models meeting post-training quality requirements. In a separate cohort, AutoResearch improved the primary task metric on held-out data for 28 of 100 production pipelines. Engineering teams estimate that the stack reduced elapsed end-to-end migration time from approximately eight weeks to two weeks, a 4x speedup.

arxiv:2610.28679.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
arxiv:2610.28679.abstract: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

arxiv:2611.00574.title: DERED: Enhancing Third-Party Library Detection in Binaries via Deceptive Reuse Mitigation
arxiv:2611.00574.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of deceptive reuse a misleading reuse relationship between recipient software that share common TPL code and proposes a novel approach, DERED, to enhance TPL detection by distinguishing between real reuse and deceptive reuse.

arxiv:2611.00628.title: AgentPRO: Coordinating Compiler Optimizations for LLM Agent Workflows
arxiv:2611.00628.abstract: LLM agents repeatedly return to a model to generate actions and interpret tool results, incurring repeated context processing and generation overhead. Yet a value needed to execute an action need not be observed by the model to generate that action. This distinction creates an optimization opportunity: reconsider where model decisions are necessary, together with the work performed between them. We present AgentPRO, a compiler framework for optimizing agent workflows as execution information becomes available. AgentPRO organizes planned duties, generation regions, and concrete operations in a hierarchical representation, distinguishing execution dependencies from observations required for generation. Region transformations combine compatible duties into fewer model requests, while operation transformations reduce redundant context and tool work. These scopes interact: eliminating a redundant read can remove an observation requirement that otherwise separates generation regions. AgentPRO coordinates transformations using initial plans, current observations, and historical execution profiles through just-in-time, adaptive, and profile-guided optimization. Runtime guards check state-dependent assumptions and retain fallback paths. We implement guarded workflow transformations for AppWorld agents. On 115 tasks selected by successful historical baseline executions, automatic AgentPRO reduces all-attempt mean token consumption by 41.85% and mean component time by 6.61% relative to those baselines, successfully completing 110 of 115 tasks.

arxiv:2611.00651.title: The Testability Gap: A Pre-Registered Census of Naming versus Implementation in 59 Cognitive-Architecture LLM Systems
arxiv:2611.00651.abstract: A companion line of work audited individual cognitive-architecture LLM systems in depth and found that module names and module computations are empirically independent claims. This paper asks how far that gap extends across the system class. We pre-registered a census protocol (sample frame, metrics, and acceptance criteria frozen before any sample was downloaded) and surveyed the 59 most-starred Python repositories declaring cognitive architecture on GitHub, plus five classic architectures as a historical control. We measure a testability gap. First, an auditability gap: 22% of repositories document no code reference whatsoever. Second, an integrity gap: 42% of repositories have at least one dangling reference, and within that subgroup the median fraction is 8%, the top quartile 19.6%, and the maximum 79.5%; one 148-star system documents paths of which a majority do not exist. Three of four pre-registered hypotheses were falsified: the integrity gap is not universal (58% of repositories either offer no checkable references or offer references that all resolve); claim density does not predict dangling rate (rho = -0.10); and the classical-architecture control does not significantly outperform (p = 0.059 with five controls, all at zero dangling). Exactly one repository in 59 (1.7%) ships executable falsification criteria for its own claims. A second pre-registered round classified every dangling path by git lifetime: 85.5% of dangling references (159 of 186) are ghosts - paths that never existed at any commit - against 14.5% that were once real and later removed.

arxiv:2611.00667.title: Characterizing and Predicting the Longest CI Builds in Machine Learning Projects
arxiv:2611.00667.abstract: Continuous integration (CI) builds in machine learning (ML) projects tend to run longer than in other projects, yet little is known about the longest builds, which consume most CI time. This paper characterizes the longest builds in ML projects, analyzes how CI workflow properties are associated with them, and evaluates whether they can be predicted before execution. We study 269,930 GitHub Actions builds from 107 open-source ML projects. The top 18% longest builds account for 80.30% of total build time and fail in 39.09% of cases. Build duration differs significantly across ML project types. The framework and infrastructure ML projects have the longest upper tail and produce 98% of the longest builds, whereas projects that use existing ML libraries have the lowest median build duration. The longest builds are most strongly associated with the recent history of the same workflow, as the duration of its last build and the median duration of the project's last 20 builds show large effect sizes. The longest builds are more consistently associated with CI workflow structure than with configuration. The number of jobs, control flow complexity, coupling complexity, and maximum steps per job show medium effect sizes, whereas caching, matrix settings, and Docker builds show small or negligible effects. Framework-specific workflows have the largest percentage of builds among long builds. Platform-specific workflows produce the largest number of the longest builds. Finally, 47 features describing build history, workflow structure, and the ML project outperform a traditional baseline with all four classifiers. In a chronological evaluation, the best model (XGBoost) reaches an F1-score of 0.775, compared with 0.682 for the baseline, and an AUC-ROC of 0.955. These results show that build history and CI workflow structure help identify the longest builds in ML projects before they run.

arxiv:2611.00689.title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages
arxiv:2611.00689.abstract: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change. We propose to govern a human-agent team through its message protocol and present yoars, a relay in which humans and agents are authenticated principals that exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an attributable, append-only record. This report gives the architecture, the full controlled study and the field material. In 926 controlled runs (899 analyzable), small agent teams built programs under varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor. Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, was followed by a drop in total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests). Instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process, and no defense inside the conversation reliably prevented the backdoor. An auditor read the records of 96 runs with a confirmed backdoor. In the 25 runs where the attacker had persuaded a teammate to write it, the auditor named the persuader in all 25, but it also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs. In a four-week field study, up to nineteen agents and two people developed a distributed system through yoars, producing 7,457 acts. Human attention and decision making emerged as the critical resource: requests waited mainly for the human-run coordinator and for approvals, while agents answered within minutes. Most governance requirements emerged from operation, and holding context dominated token cost. We report twenty-six failures of our own instruments, derive seven lessons and a checklist, and release the corpus, the redacted room ledger and the analysis scripts.

arxiv:2611.00707.title: Verification-Gated Redraw and Repair for Local Small Language Models: A Paired Evaluation
arxiv:2611.00707.abstract: Executable checks can reject incorrect model-generated programs, but rejection alone does not determine whether fresh sampling or diagnostic repair is preferable. We present a controlled, resource-bounded conceptual replication and extension of established recovery policies: a single answer (N), one verification-triggered redraw (R), and one diagnostic repair (D), for Ornith 1.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B served locally in nominal 4-bit MLX format. The frozen evaluation contains 72 tasks: 40 HumanEval+ problems, 16 SQL tasks and 16 shell tasks. Policies share initial responses and use only public checks for online decisions; every candidate is model-generated. Each task has one stochastic trajectory per model, so the study does not estimate variation across independent sampling blocks. Redraw increases observed final-test success from 51.4% to 59.7% for Ornith and from 55.6% to 62.5% for Gemma. Diagnostic repair reaches 52.8% and 63.9%, respectively. None of four internally prespecified paired contrasts is significant after Holm correction (minimum adjusted p = 0.125). Public checks falsely accept 25 Ornith and 11 Gemma candidates, demonstrating that acceptance is not a correctness guarantee. A post-review audit of initial answers gives perfect-retry upper bounds of 76.4% and 87.5%, respectively: accepted initial errors cannot trigger recovery under the fixed gate. This one-block, resource-bounded study provides a finite-cohort experimental record, not policy equivalence, a general model ranking or universal reliability

arxiv:2611.00723.title: Architecting Fairness-Aware LLM Interactions
arxiv:2611.00723.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools but may generate stereotypical, discriminatory, or unfair responses. As LLMs become embedded in decision-critical software systems, fairness can no longer be treated as a downstream evaluation step, but must become an architectural concern of the interaction itself. Yet current fairness approaches operate as standalone evaluation techniques, lacking a reusable mechanism to verify and mitigate violations at runtime. We propose a fairness-assurance architecture grounded in three reusable design patterns, instantiated as a multi-agent framework that evaluates and iteratively refines LLM responses before delivery. A preliminary evaluation across eight configurations involving different LLM families shows that the architecture identifies fairness violations and iteratively produces compliant responses in all configurations, with behavior differing depending on the model-family composition. These results provide initial evidence for the joint instantiation of the proposed patterns and a first step toward architecting non-functional properties into LLM-based systems.

arxiv:2611.00944.title: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
arxiv:2611.00944.abstract: Modern software systems expose hundreds of configuration options whose combinations can substantially affect execution time, memory and energy usage. Measuring software performance resulting from a configuration set requires running a realistic workload. Since the configuration space grows exponentially, exhaustive benchmarking is infeasible. Prior work therefore trains models on a small set of measured configurations to predict the performance of the rest. Yet these models are specific to a particular software version, hardware platform, and workload, so changes require new measurements and retraining, and such changes are becoming more frequent with coding agents. We challenge this per-system training assumption with SNAPPERF (Software-aware, No-retraining, Adaptive Prediction), a sample-efficient tabular foundation model specialized for configurable software. SNAPPERF is pretrained once on synthetic data. Each new update only requires a few measured configurations as context to predict the rest without any per-system training or hyperparameter tuning. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, spanning 6 domains and 4 performance metrics, SNAPPERF reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same measurement budget, and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model. It matches the state of the art's accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average. These results suggest that knowledge about software can be encoded in pretraining data rather than in per-system models, opening a new research direction in software-aware pretraining.

arxiv:2611.01043.title: Dependable Agents Need Hard and Fuzzy Rules
arxiv:2611.01043.abstract: Language models let software read requests in ordinary language, but they keep rules as people do: usually, and less so under pressure. Conventional code keeps rules exactly, but it cannot read a request. We argue that dependable agents need both, because the two kinds of rule cover overlapping and unequal regions of what an agent might do. Code holds the limits that can be stated exactly. Learned fuzzy rules cover the judgment that cannot. We test the hard layer in three domains, purchasing, delegation of authority and data access, on 1,340 episodes written by authors outside our team. Models left to decide for themselves executed unauthorized actions in up to 151 of 340 purchasing episodes and 269 of 470 delegation episodes, and the strongest model breached in every condition. A hard guard between proposal and action executed none, and an exhaustive search of 183,204 proposals agreed. In a further test, where an outsider wrote the owner's rules and a program mapped them to the guard, two episodes breached at a boundary we had written down in advance. We then test the pair. Concept Programming instills a named rule in a model and measures its errors on wording it never saw. A small model taught four judgment rules this way flagged 95 of 96 rule-breaking purchases that no exact rule can see, and 4 of 108 legitimate requests. Placed in front of the guard, it left 1 of 192 rule-breaking requests unstopped, where the guard alone left 77 and 70, and the guard still held every exact limit. A prompted frontier model did about as well, so the claim is that a small taught rule can do the job, not that it does it better.

arxiv:2611.01127.title: What Must Be Done Here? Using a Bounded Application-Security Ontology at the Point of Change
arxiv:2611.01127.abstract: The security guidance that bears on code is real but scattered. It lives across secure-development frameworks, verification standards, controls catalogues, threat taxonomies, and, increasingly, normative regimes such as the EU's NIS2 -- and most of it is written for readers other than the engineer, or the AI assistant, at a point of change. Existing cybersecurity ontologies largely model attacks, indicators, and risk for detection and analysis, not the engineering-practice substance one must act on. This paper presents a use case for an existing bounded application-security ontology, AppSec Core, whose construction and validation are reported separately. We show how it is used. It makes the engineering-actionable fraction of those authorities addressable as a typed working set: the control objectives that apply, the practices that realize them, the mechanisms that implement them, and the evidence artifacts they expect, each traceable to the sources that justify it. We reach that working set from two entry points that recur in practice. Forward, from a code change: a change to authentication middleware scopes to its governing domain slice and returns the obligations the change must satisfy. Inverse, from a normative obligation: "make this NIS2-compliant" resolves a generic legal duty into the concrete engineering obligations it implies across slices, surfacing precisely the fraction of a mostly-governance regulation that lands in code. The same working set is what a human engineer reads and what an LLM-grounded assistant is handed as grounding. The use turns "read every applicable authority" into "satisfy this typed working set", for a code change or a compliance duty alike. The contribution is the demonstrated use; the artefact, its validation, and its governance are companion work.

arxiv:2611.01173.title: From Stories to Bugs: Story-Based Semantic Fuzzing of Interactive Systems
arxiv:2611.01173.abstract: Complex interactive systems hide business-logic failures along two complementary axes: deep state-dependent behaviors that require long valid prefixes and concurrency-sensitive failures that depend on the ordering of otherwise legal operations. We present story-based semantic fuzzing, a methodology that treats semantically constrained compositions of behavioral stories as primary search objects. Implemented through Behavioral Programming, semantic binding and state constraints preserve legal prefixes, while event eligibility, schedule selection, and replay expose failure-relevant interleavings. We evaluate the methodology on Magento and four stateful REST APIs. On Magento, overlap-aware ranking increased reproduction of a sporadic Shipping Fee race from 3.6% to 41.2%; a controlled ordering intervention reduced a second failure signature from 100/100 initial executions to 0/200 constrained executions. For the REST study, a versioned end-to-end pipeline took each frozen public OpenAPI contract as its sole benchmark-specific model-generation input and automatically generated the Basic and Complex stories, dependency structure, and interface bindings. Under a shared black-box task and sequence-local evaluation contract, Basic and Complex confirmed 0/11 and 11/11 semantic fault classes, while RESTler and EvoMaster confirmed 2/11 and 0/11. A paired binding ablation produced 250/250 valid dependent operations with binding and 0/250 without it, while supplementary prefix controls localized the difference to preservation of legal relational state. Together, the studies show that searching admissible semantic compositions provides a unified and effective representation for reaching deep states and exposing concurrency-sensitive business-logic failures.

arxiv:2611.01181.title: Do Coding Agents Catch Their Own Bugs? (They Don't.)
arxiv:2611.01181.abstract: In software development, engineers need to foresee and fix potential problems with their code that are not explicitly specified in requirements---such as pre-emptively considering vulnerabilities or other bugs from a code change. But current benchmarks often do not measure these future-looking consequences. We introduce $\textbf{Foresight-SWE}$, a benchmark for measuring whether coding agents can anticipate and address unstated problems during software engineering tasks. Foresight-SWE consists of 212 samples spanning 4 languages and 35 popular open-source repositories. Each sample contains two pull requests (PRs), the second of which resolves defects the first one introduced. To measure whether agents exhibit foresight, we define the $\textbf{foresight resolve rate (FRR)}$ as the fraction of instances where an agent fully resolves the original task while also avoiding the defect identified by a later PR. We evaluate eleven large language models and find that FRR ranges from only 6.13% to 24.53%, indicating that models largely fail to address problems introduced by the first PR change. This raises important questions about how models are trained and aligned in coding contexts, as well as how code review tools should be improved for more fail-safe coding. Foresight-SWE shifts evaluations in this direction.

arxiv:2611.01196.title: A Domain Driven Design Based Reference Architecture for IoT Systems Engineering
arxiv:2611.01196.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm continues to gain significant traction across diverse do-mains, primarily driven by its transformative and socio-economic benefits. However, engineering robust IoT systems remains a formidable challenge, largely due to the inherent dynamism, volatility, and uncertainty of their operational environments. To mitigate this architectural complexity, microservices have emerged as a viable alternative to traditional, rigid monolithic frameworks, offering a scalable mechanism to fulfill critical quality attributes. To maximize the efficacy of a microservices architecture, its technical boundaries must align precisely with domain-specific business requirements. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) addresses this need by strategically decomposing complex domains into modular, highly manageable subdomains that map directly to individual microservices. Furthermore, to minimize architectural coupling, enhance system integrability, and optimize device energy efficiency, Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) serves as a critical operational enabler. This paper proposes a comprehensive reference architecture for IoT systems engineering, systematically leveraging DDD and EDA principles to harmonize business logic with decoupled, event-driven microservices.

arxiv:2611.01255.title: AdapBench: Adaptive Early-Stopping and Prioritization for Efficient Microbenchmarking in Cloud-based CI/CD
arxiv:2611.01255.abstract: Cloud-based software systems frequently release new versions, a fact further accelerated through agentic coding. Each new release, however, brings the risk of performance regressions which can irritate end users, increase infrastructure costs, and increase carbon footprints. Therefore, developers strive to catch such regressions in testing stages, usually through so-called continuous benchmarking. The standard way of doing this is using microbenchmark suites which, however, take notoriously long to execute. Optimizing the execution of microbenchmark suites is, hence, an active field of research. In this paper, we propose AdapBench, an online scheduling system for reducing the execution duration of microbenchmark suites. AdapBench is the first approach which dynamically makes at-runtime decisions for prioritizing the most informative benchmarks and early-stopping each one once enough evidence has accumulated to accept or reject a performance change hypothesis. We evaluate our prototype on eight popular Java projects, commonly used by microbenchmark research, and four additional Go projects. At matched 90% change detections and false-positive rate compared to an optimistic uniform run, AdapBench saves 42% of the aggregate execution duration on the Java projects, with negligible scheduling overhead (below 0.001% of the total runtime). On the Go projects, AdapBench finds every performance change with zero false positives while saving 85% of the full run.

arxiv:2611.01265.title: Toward Bounding Coding-Agent Autonomy in Software Maintenance: A Pilot Study of Boundary Contracts
arxiv:2611.01265.abstract: As coding agents gain greater autonomy to modify software repositories, relevant context alone does not define their operational authority. An artifact may be relevant to a maintenance task while being inappropriate to edit; conversely, another artifact may be required even when it is not explicitly mentioned in the request. We explore Boundary Contracts, a machine-readable abstraction that makes task-specific artifact roles (editable, inspect-only, required, and protected) explicit before repository modification begins. We conduct a pilot study on 40 maintenance tasks from a real enterprise repository, comparing the same Codex-based coding agent with and without Boundary Contract information. The boundary-informed condition improves macro edit-selection F1 from 0.440 to 0.682, required-behavior coverage from 0.429 to 0.673, and the number of strictly acceptable patches from 9 of 40 to 18 of 40. To probe whether these gains are explained only by improved file localization, we additionally analyze 21 tasks in which both conditions modify at least one identical file. Differences remain in edit selectivity and patch outcomes, providing initial evidence that explicit artifact roles may influence maintenance behavior beyond localization alone. This pilot does not establish the general effectiveness of Boundary Contracts. Rather, it provides initial evidence for a broader research question: how should the operational boundaries of coding agents be generated, validated, revised, and ultimately enforced as repository-level maintenance becomes increasingly autonomous?

arxiv:2611.01292.title: Causality-Based Fault Localization
arxiv:2611.01292.abstract: We introduce Causality-Based Fault Localization (CBFL), a novel approach to fault localization grounded in the theory of actual causality. We use the notion of causal responsibility to formalize and define the contribution of a given location in the source code under the context of a failing test. We also utilize a distance metric to prioritize minimal fixes and penalize broken tests, leading to more interpretable and fixable fault localization. We implemented CBFL in a tool, SoftReX, and our evaluation results demonstrate that SoftReX outperforms state-of-the-art Mutation-Based Fault Localization (MBFL) tools based on Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Top-1 by 16% on both metrics, when using the same set of mutants. We also propose a sophisticated mutation generation strategy based on the structure and representation of the program to improve the accuracy of our ranked list, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 2.6x in terms of required mutants evaluated while remaining competitive in performance.

arxiv:2611.01357.title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
arxiv:2611.01357.abstract: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.

arxiv:2611.01358.title: WFDB-x: Conformance-Tested Implementations of the WFDB Software Package in Seven Programming Languages
arxiv:2611.01358.abstract: The WFDB format is widely used to store and exchange physiological waveforms and annotations. However, existing software implementations are limited to C, Python, and MATLAB/Octave, can produce different results in corner cases and checksum calculations, and have defaults such as sampling frequency and gain, that can lead to silent misinterpretation of recordings. We developed WFDB-x, a cross-language, performance-optimized reimplementation of WFDB in seven programming languages, with extensive unit tests, to provide consistent WFDB processing across programming languages. We reimplemented the WFDB Software Package 10.7.0 natively in Python, C++, Rust, Julia, R, MATLAB/Octave, and Kotlin, using AI-assistance under human direction and review. Each implementation has library functions, a high-level interface, and command-line tools. We compared their outputs with those of the original C programs using 1098 conformance cases, 877 legacy-mode cases, unit tests, and differential fuzzing. Deliberate changes remove implicit waveform parameters, restrict file and network access, and prevent annotation loss. A legacy mode retains the original behavior. All seven implementations passed every conformance and legacy-mode case on the tested Linux platform, with matching outputs. The unit tests contain 9353 assertions. C++, Rust, and Julia read records 1.5-6.9 times faster than the original C library, while the Python implementation wrote records 9.2 times faster than the existing wfdb-python library in the benchmark. WFDB-x provides a tested, open-source basis for reading and writing physiological recordings consistently across seven languages, supporting reproducible research and software development without requiring a shared programming environment. We also share details of the AI-assisted development process and token utilization, which may be useful for other applications.

arxiv:2611.01377.title: A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development
arxiv:2611.01377.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit powerful code generation abilities, fostering agentic systems to automate edge AI application development. However, existing agents typically operate via fixed agentic workflows and predefined design spaces, struggling to handle rapidly evolving demands of real-world scenarios (e.g., heterogeneous data modalities, diverse task pipelines). Unlike prior systems that treat LLMs mainly as code generators following rigid workflows, we fully exploit their reasoning capabilities to allow agents to determine their own workflows on the fly. To this end, we propose SE2, a self-exploring and self-evolving paradigm for adaptive edge AI development. Inspired by human learning processes, we distill development into four atomic operations (retrieve, reason, code, test), and empower agents to explore workflows by dynamically and adaptively selecting an appropriate next operation based on the current context. Extensive evaluations show that, with adaptive workflows, the synthesized programs achieve up to 26% higher accuracy and consume 28% lower resources than state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability to unforeseen edge AI scenarios. This highlights the potential of reasoning-driven adaptive agentic workflow in edge AI development.

arxiv:2611.01383.title: Toward Executable Multi-framework Front-end Code Generation with Self-Correction
arxiv:2611.01383.abstract: Generating codes from UI screenshots has recently benefited from MLLMs, yet existing methods centered on HTML targets and transfer poorly to multi-frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular. However, unlike HTML, which does not entail compilation issues, generating executable code in multi-framework settings is more challenging due to framework-specific differences in syntax and failure modes, as well as the need to maintain global consistency across files. To address this problem, we study executable multi-framework front-end code generation and propose MESCoder, a tree-structured self-corrective generation framework. Our method first extracts a structural scaffold from the screenshot and then constructs sub-trees and assembly relations step by step, transforming large project generation into a sequence of localized decisions. On top of this scaffold, we introduce a unified Project Agent that continuously revises its own partial project under runtime sandbox feedback and dynamically chooses between local repair and cluster level repair. For training, we adopt a two-stage strategy that first initializes the policy offline to learn basic multi-framework generation and repair priors, and then refines it with online reinforcement learning to optimize long horizon executability and final page quality. The resulting framework models multi-framework executability as a conditioned project state transition process and improves the stability and quality of complex front end generation through self correction. Experiments show that our method improves executability, while narrowing the visual-fidelity gap to HTML-based generation. Code is available at https://github.com/leo-lilinxiao/MESCoder.

arxiv:2610.38311.title: Detecting Incorrect LLM Explanations for Automated Program Repair
arxiv:2610.38311.abstract: LLM-generated explanations help developers understand automated program repair (APR) rationale and assess patch quality. Incorrect explanations can mislead developers about a repair's reliability, making their detection important. However, manually inspecting the growing volume of generated repairs is impractical, motivating automated detection. Existing methods mainly target incorrect answers from general question-answering LLMs, often by sampling multiple responses and detecting contradictions. Applied to APR, they face two limitations: (1) they may depend on external verifiers that are unavailable or lack APR-specific reasoning; and (2) sampling strategies such as paraphrasing or re-prompting the same input often yield superficial, redundant responses that repeat the original error rather than expose it. We propose MetaReJ, the first method designed to detect incorrect APR explanations using metamorphic testing. Inspired by debate and viva examinations, MetaReJ challenges explanations through an argumentative strategy without requiring external verifiers. It applies novel metamorphic relations (MRs) to recursively question the LLM under equivalent and non-equivalent repair scenarios and detect contradictions. To obtain diverse samples, MetaReJ transforms the buggy program into variants that preserve or alter the underlying bug, then asks the LLM how to repair each variant. Contradictions among responses are encoded as MR violations, which indicate that the original explanation is incorrect. We evaluate MetaReJ on a manually labelled dataset of 1,756 explanations from multiple LLM-based APR systems. MetaReJ achieves an MCC of up to 0.43, outperforming prior methods by up to 333.3% in MCC.

arxiv:2611.01572.title: Impossible Code, Barely Changed Score: A Replay Study of Judge-Based Evaluation
arxiv:2611.01572.abstract: Language models are often used to judge generated code without running it. A useful evaluation should reveal substantial changes in the answers it scores. We examine this requirement by repeating an earlier evaluation on 421 coding problems, comparing Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct with two versions trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). One receives rewards from execution tests (CE-trained), and the other from a strong language-model judge (SLJ-trained). The base model's syntax-failure rate remains stable, but the trained checkpoints produce invalid Python on 63%-67% of attempts. Despite this change, the strong judge's Pass@32 scores fall by only about 3 percentage points, from 96.67% to 93.95% for SLJ-trained. Within the later run, allowing more attempts makes the base and trained checkpoints look increasingly similar under the judge. With 128 attempts per question, the judge accepts at least one SLJ-trained answer on 96.44% of problems, compared with 28.27% under execution tests. We recommend reporting the share of answers that pass Python's syntax check alongside every judge-based score. This check requires no tests or code execution and flags invalid answers that the judge accepts, although it cannot establish functional correctness. Our findings show how a high judge-based score can hide substantial output damage and motivate checking an evaluation's sensitivity to change. Project page and code: https://curiousorbitnotes.github.io/evorobust-replay-audit/

arxiv:2611.01636.title: What reviewers call a Long Method is a length: A pre-registered test of coupling divergence as a god-unit signal, and what it settled instead
arxiv:2611.01636.abstract: A companion study found that a complexity outlier rule shows where complexity concentrates but cannot tell a god unit from a complex algorithm. This paper pre-registered a test of one way to tell them apart: weight a unit's complexity by its coupling divergence, the data it hands on minus the data it receives, so that a leaf is set aside. Coupling was measured by resolving every call in 520 MLCQ repositories, 500 fresh Java repositories and 73 Qualitas Corpus systems. The claim fails: the primary, the pooled MCC of the weighted form minus complexity alone against MLCQ's human Blob, is -0.041 [-0.130, +0.054], no difference resolved and underpowered, and the resolved readings go against it. What the data settle is at method level. What MLCQ's reviewers call a Long Method is an absolute length: a constant of 26 lines or more, chosen on the explore half, reaches MCC 0.777 on the confirm half, +0.080 [+0.016, +0.145] over the best per-repository form; every reviewer with ten or more positives, on their non-leaf reviews, has a best cutoff between 17 and 34 lines; and nothing measured inside a method, its calls, variables, data flow or the cost of cutting it, refines the constant. The constant is a limit of human reading. The next form of the construct is the cost of bringing a long method under it, which is where the construct meets architecture.

arxiv:2611.01692.title: Phase-wise MLLM Tuning for Multi-framework WebUI Code Generation
arxiv:2611.01692.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance in translating WebUI screenshots into HTML/CSS. However, when they faced multiple frameworks (React/Vue/Angular), they often suffer from negative transfer that leads to compilation failures. These failures commonly stem from mixing framework specific syntax and violating framework constraints. This paper studies supervised fine-tuning for multi-framework WebUI code generation and proposes a phase-wise MLLM tuning method driven by compatibility and heterogeneity signals across frameworks. We first apply a normalization mapping that preserves each framework's native syntax while suppressing noise from variable naming and literal content. We then estimate cross framework heterogeneity and compatibility offline, and automatically derive training groups and their ordering by maximizing a phased objective. Finally, we perform phase-wise adapter tuning to reduce cross framework interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our proposed method improves both generation quality and compilation success rate compared with baselines.

arxiv:2611.01743.title: VeriBase: Automated Construction of Theorem Libraries for Software Verification
arxiv:2611.01743.abstract: Software verification is typically more challenging than coding. Software developers routinely build on mature libraries and APIs, but turning successful verification solutions into reusable libraries still requires substantial expert effort. In this paper, we propose VeriBase, a framework for automatically constructing software-verification libraries by jointly generalizing code and its associated theorems from successful verification solutions. The key challenge is to generalize implementations together with the theorem statements and proofs that depend on these implementations, and reconcile overlapping components across verification tasks. To this end, VeriBase treats code and its associated theorems as declaration families, and designs a three-phase pipeline, which proves seed tasks, generalizes code and associated theorems, and harvests the resulting families into shared interfaces. VeriBase updates dependent declarations as interface change and uses Lean to check the resulting code and proofs. We evaluate VeriBase across four benchmarks with three backend LLMs. The results show that the general-purpose library built from independent 4,191 programs increases the average task success rate by up to 17.0% and meanwhile reduces the proof completion time by up to 21.4%. When VeriBase constructs a benchmark-specific library, further improvement can be observed.

arxiv:2611.01930.title: RECEIPT: Measuring and Repairing the Return Assumption of LLM Agents in Web Service Operations
arxiv:2611.01930.abstract: LLM agents operate Web infrastructure from the command line and rely on a return assumption, namely that each tool call returns within a bounded time and with its requested action finished. Many commands, however, ask a question before they act, and the agent's harness either closes the program's input or keeps it open as a terminal at which nobody types. With closed input, the program can return status 0 without the requested action. With open input, it waits until a time limit, and the agent pays in time and tokens. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to measure and repair the return assumption. We collect 91,469 production tool calls and 89,047 public agent trajectories, test how 8 widely used harnesses launch commands, and build Litmus, a catalog of 158 checked command-line invocations, and Tripwire, a benchmark of 25 task pairs that differ only in whether a question guards the requested action. We then propose RECEIPT, which keeps the input open, reads what each process waits for from system calls, and returns this state to an unmodified agent through a model-checked protocol. On Litmus, closed input causes 11.5% of tested invocations to return status 0 without performing the requested action, and 7 of 8 harnesses close input when no terminal is attached. An unanswered question at a plain terminal multiplies a task's token use by 2.9, and the input connection moves an LLM from 7th to 3rd place among 8. Across 5 LLMs, RECEIPT reduces false claims of success by 73.5% and completes all 25 guarded tasks on a second harness. An agent's reliability therefore depends on what its harness lets it observe as well as on its LLM. Agent builders should report what each tool call did, not only how it ended, and benchmark maintainers should fix and report the input connection before they rank LLMs.

arxiv:2611.01953.title: Step-Zero Attack: Agent Safety Before Observability
arxiv:2611.01953.abstract: Existing attacks and defenses for coding agents act once content enters the model context: injected text persuades the model, and guards inspect what the model reads. Yet to judge whether processing an unknown archive, network response, or image is safe, an agent often must process it first, and that step can do harm before any content reaches the model. We call this first processing Step Zero, and harm done by it a Step-Zero attack. Across seven harnesses and six models, each agent received only a path or URL to a crafted input, paired with a benign twin showing the same visible fields. Step Zero is where most agents are already unsafe: 32/42 harness-model pairs overran a 4 MiB disk budget, 26/42 before the model saw any member, and four of the six models did so in every round (84/84), so the damage precedes any model-side defense. Every twin stayed within budget, so the attacker's bytes alone cause the harm. On network and image inputs the risk moves to what the agent writes: agents stored the body under the name the input declared, letting the input decide what is written, and their checks faded once cues were removed. Model-free tests trace the harm to the processing primitive, so we defend it there: a gate that counts the bytes each call produces held every routed extraction within budget while agents completed 25/28 tasks. Vendors should pair such gates with safety-alignment training that teaches agents to inspect an input before processing it.

arxiv:2611.01966.title: Launder-Bench: Can Repository-Level Agentic Code Laundering Be Detected?
arxiv:2611.01966.abstract: Coding agents can now rewrite repository-scale codebases while preserving tested behavior, creating a new challenge for plagiarism detection, license auditing, and software provenance. We ask whether such rewrites can still be traced to their source. Existing clone benchmarks emphasize fragments and bounded edits, while repository-transformation benchmarks evaluate functional correctness rather than provenance. Moreover, ranking the most similar source does not establish derivation when independent implementations can be similarly close. We define repository-level agentic code laundering and introduce Launder-Bench, to our knowledge the first repository-level benchmark for provenance under agentic rewriting, constructed from 282 real-world repositories. A source-hidden reconstruction protocol decomposes source behavior, reconstructs modules and repository structure, and retains rewrites only after execution-based verification. We evaluate the same provenance problem in two complementary settings: Launder-Bench-Pair contains 1,128 pairwise instances asking whether two repositories share provenance, while Launder-Bench-Attr contains 229 source-attribution instances asking which candidate is the source, with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Measured same-domain independent repositories establish how much similarity can arise without shared provenance and provide detector-specific reference bands. Existing methods remain far from saturating Launder-Bench: the strongest static method reaches only 0.66 AUROC on pairwise detection, while repository encoders rank the true source first on up to 22% of attribution queries but earn calibrated attribution credit on only 1-2%. These results reveal a systematic gap between relative code similarity and source-specific provenance evidence, providing a reproducible target for provenance detection under agentic rewriting.

arxiv:2611.02074.title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
arxiv:2611.02074.abstract: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.

arxiv:2611.02125.title: Semantic Interoperability in Federated Digital Twin Systems: A Systematic Review Through the Levels of Conceptual Interoperability Model
arxiv:2611.02125.abstract: When two companies connect their digital twins, software models of their plants kept up to date with live data, each twin must translate the other's data into its own terms, and that translation rule, called a mapping, can stop being correct when one company changes the meaning of its data without telling the other. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review screened 5,833 records and read 119 full texts to determine whether any published system detects such a broken mapping and repairs it while the twins operate. In all 32 included studies the mapping is fixed before operation, and the two ingredients of run-time repair appear only separately: cross-company matching without any check that the match still holds, and detection and repair of changed meaning within a single company. The review turns this gap into six requirements, each illustrated on one running example, that a system claiming run-time semantic interoperability between independently owned twins should meet.

arxiv:2611.02155.title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
arxiv:2611.02155.abstract: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.

arxiv:2611.02207.title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
arxiv:2611.02207.abstract: Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent requests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-Bench, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they complete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external ``that's wrong'' after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions.

arxiv:2611.02251.title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
arxiv:2611.02251.abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.

arxiv:2611.02285.title: Modern Software Engineering with Verification Agents: A Spec-First Architecture for Autonomous Synthesis, Verification IRs, and Organizational Scale
arxiv:2611.02285.abstract: When autonomous coding agents synthesize implementation code, formal specifications, and mechanical proofs simultaneously, the software engineering hierarchy inverts: the formal specification becomes the primary human-reviewed artifact, while source code and proof scripts become disposable build outputs. This paper presents an end-to-end architecture for agent-authored, formally verified software engineering. First, we establish a logic-agnostic foundation combining a spec-first stack inversion, a zero-code-review workflow gated by automated continuous integration (CI) checks, and a minimal Verification Intermediate Representation (VIR) lowered via a thin, verified translator. Second, we pair an extensional Computational Type Theory (CTT) specification layer with Higher-Order Abstract Syntax (HOAS) and linear resource typing in the VIR--eliminating rewrite friction for synthesis agents while defining an experiment, its protocol frozen before the first reader, to measure whether removing boundary coercions improves human specification readability.
